summary: The note describes a local surge in outdoor "green exercise" since September 2023, driven by instructors, community organizers, schools, and local government. It cites research and expert comments linking outdoor activity to better energy, lower stress, social connection, mental health, and environmental appreciation. It also covers tech integration, urban green space barriers, and a call to move workouts outdoors.
one_line: Local residents are shifting to outdoor green exercise, supported by research, community programs, schools, technology, and new green space projects, with physical, mental, and environmental benefits.
key_facts: Green exercise is physical activity in the presence of nature, and it has been gaining traction among health professionals and the public since September 2023.
A study released in October 2023 by Dr. Emily Forrest of the University Health Network found outdoor exercisers report higher energy and lower stress than indoor exercisers.
Fitness instructor Marcus Johnson moved most of his classes from his studio to local parks since the summer of 2023.
Community organizer Sarah Thomson coordinated the "Green Fitness Days," which debuted in September 2023 and offer free outdoor classes from yoga to HIIT.
Since the start of the 2023-24 school year, local schools have incorporated more outdoor physical education classes.
Physical education teacher Jacob Lee reports students are more engaged and excited when classes are held outside.

The "Youth Outdoor League," founded by local parents in November 2023, gets children into outdoor team sports like soccer and baseball, whereas most leagues previously played in domes or indoor arenas.
Personal trainer Anne Kim livestreams her outdoor workout sessions for clients.
Accessibility of green spaces in urban areas is a challenge, and the River Park Fitness Trail is slated to open by the end of 2024.
Environmental advocate Dylan Matthews says people who spend more time outdoors develop greater appreciation for nature and contribute to conservation.
Psychiatrist Dr. Linda Singh says outdoor exercise can reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, with sunlight raising vitamin D levels linked to mood regulation.
Apps that track outdoor runs, manage hiking trails, or simulate outdoor cycling routes have become increasingly popular.
